name: Tipra
confidence_why: Chakraborty 1981 (fieldwork in Tripura) describes Tipra as tonal with four tones and no fixed word stress, and Joseph & Burling 2001 independently confirm a tonal contrast for Kokborok, including a low-functional-load high tone in a Bangladesh dialect; the sources differ only on the number of tones, and Kim et al. 2011 leave the tone status of the Bangladesh varieties open, so the tonal classification has a clear winner from few sources.

D.Phil. thesis, University of Burdwan (Glottolog dates it 1982); printed Agartala: Tribal Research and Cultural Institute, Government of Tripura. 112 pp. In Bengali. Open scan: archive.org;gov.tribals.75014.
catalog_locator: Phonology chapter, p. 16 (archive.org leaf 28; scan); tone discussion pp. 14-15 (leaf 27).
catalog_quote: পূর্বেই উল্লেখ করেছি যে, তিপ্রা ভাষায় ঝোঁক বর্তমান। এই ঝোঁক ইংরাজী কিংবা বাংলা ভাষার শ্বাসাঘাতের মতো নয়। ইংরাজী ভাষায় প্রত্যেক মূল শব্দের নিজস্ব শ্বাসাঘাত আছে এবং বাক্যের প্রত্যেক মৌলিক শব্দ স্বকীয় শ্বাসাঘাত শুদ্ধ নিজ স্বাতন্ত্র্য বজায় রাখে। বাংলায় একক উচ্চারণে শব্দে আদি শ্বাসাঘাত; ... তিপ্রা ভাষার বাক্প্রবাহে শ্বাসাঘাত পড়ে দু'ভাবে। এক, শব্দবিশেষে। যেমন, 'ডিম' অর্থে | তক্তুই | বা | তাখুম্তুই | ব্যবহার না করে যদি | বুতুই | শব্দ ব্যবহার করা হয় তবে প্রায় সমোচ্চারিত 'ঝোল' বাচক | বুতুই | শব্দের সঙ্গে পৃথকীকরণের জন্য 'ডিম' বাচক | বুতুই | শব্দের আদিতে একটি ঝোঁকের ব্যবহার আবশ্যিক হয়ে পড়ে। দুই, পর্বের অন্ত্যস্বরে যদি ক্রিয়ার কাল জ্ঞাপক প্রত্যয়, কারক-বিভক্তি কিংবা অব্যয় থাকে তবে সেই অন্ত্যস্বরে একটি ঝোঁক পড়ে। শ্বাস পর্বের অন্ত্যস্বরে স্থানবিশেষে ঝোঁক, ক্ষেত্রবিশেষে স্বরের ওঠা-নামা এবং প্রসূত-উচ্চারণ রীতির সঙ্গে সঙ্গত স্বরের ব্যবহার তিপ্রা ভাষাকে এক বিশেষ শ্রুতি-মাধুর্য দান করেছে।

new_statements.translation: I have already mentioned that stress (jhõk) exists in the Tipra language. This stress is not like the stress (śvāsāghāt) of English or of Bengali. [...] In Tipra connected speech, stress falls in two ways. One, on particular words: e.g. if for 'egg' one uses |butui| rather than |toktui| or |takhumtui|, then, to keep it apart from the nearly homophonous |butui| 'broth', a stress at the beginning of the word |butui| 'egg' becomes obligatory. Two, if the final vowel of a (breath-)group carries a verbal tense suffix, a case ending or a particle, then a stress falls on that final vowel.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed lexical word-stress position. The author (who also describes four pitch patterns/tones with occasional lexical function, pp.14-15, and says stress is gaining ground over tone) states that Tipra stress is unlike English per-word stress or Bengali initial stress: prominence is (a) word-initial on certain lexical items to disambiguate near-homophones, and (b) on the last vowel of a breath group when that vowel is a tense suffix, case marker or particle, i.e. right-edge, suffix-bearing prominence at the phrase level. (For Kokborok proper, Veikho & Mushahary 2015:166 report instrumentally that in disyllables stress is always on the second syllable, consistent with right-edge prominence.)
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically specified initial stress on some words used to separate near-homophones (bútui 'egg' vs butui 'broth'); otherwise none.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly connected speech: the unit is the শ্বাসপর্ব 'breath group' within the utterance (বাক্প্রবাহ); the author contrasts this with English word-level stress, so the statement is phrase-level, not about citation forms. Impressionistic; the same author argues in his preface that Tipra is 'not tone-based' and possibly Austroasiatic, so the source is idiosyncratic.
new_statements.identity_note: tipp1239 'Tippera' [tpe] is the Glottolog/Ethnologue entry for the Kok Borok speech of the Tripura people of Bangladesh (Chittagong Hill Tracts, Khagrachari etc.); per Kim et al. 2011 most Bangladesh Tripura speak non-Debbarma varieties (e.g. Naitong/Khagrachari types) related to but distinct from standard (Debbarma, Agartala) Kok Borok = kokb1239, with Usoi [usi] and Riang [ria] coded separately, and even the tonal status of the Bangladesh varieties is unverified. The quoted source, Chakraborty 1981, describes 'Tipra' = Kokborok of Tripura state, India, explicitly without dialect differentiation (effectively the standard language, kokb1239); Glottolog files it under tipp1239. No phonological description specific to Bangladesh Tippera was found; the sibling folder holds the India-side Kokborok sources (incl. Veikho & Mushahary 2015 with a second-syllable stress statement).

new_statements.translation: I have already noted that Tipra has stress (jhõk). This stress is not like the stress (śvāsāghāt) of English or Bengali. [...] In the Tipra flow of speech, stress falls in two ways. One, on particular words: for example, if for 'egg' one uses |butui| rather than |taktui| or |takhumtui|, then, to keep it apart from the almost identically pronounced |butui| meaning 'broth', a stress on the beginning of |butui| 'egg' becomes obligatory. new_statements.rule_in_words: Tipra has both tone (স্বর) and stress (ঝোঁক / শ্বাসাঘাত). Tone: four tones (rising, falling, falling-rising, low; no high tone), and word meaning sometimes depends on tone (p. 15). Stress is not word-fixed as in English or Bengali; in connected speech it falls in two ways: (1) lexically, on the initial of particular words to keep near-homophones apart (butui 'egg' gets initial stress to distinguish it from butui 'broth'); (2) on the final syllable of a breath-group when that syllable is a tense suffix, case ending or particle (p. 16). No general word-level placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is explicitly said not to be a fixed word-stress like English or Bengali; lexical (disambiguating) initial stress on specific words vs. phrase-final stress on suffixes/case endings/particles. p. 15 adds that as suffixation and borrowing grow, the language is drifting away from tone toward stress, and that many homophones cannot be separated by tone alone but by stress, affixation and sentence position. The introductory chapter also asserts (the scanned textpage not verified on image) that although many words are tonal, 'the language is not tone-based either' (ভাষাটি সুরাশ্রিতও নয়), in tension with p. 15.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog tipp1239 'Tippera' (ISO tpe) is the Bangladesh side of the Kok Borok complex; the catalog names the entry 'Tipra'. Chakraborty 1981 describes 'Tipra' = the Kok-Borok dialects of the eight tribes (Tipra, Riang, Jamatia, Rupini, Noatia, Kalai, Uchai, Murasing) of Tripura State, India, from fieldwork in Tripura with monolingual informants, without dialect differentiation; Glottolog files it under tipp1239 but it is in substance a description of Indian Kokborok (kokb1239). Joseph & Burling's Kokborok data are from P. Jamatia of Tripura (India); only the compilers footnotes 11 and 13 (Matisoff) concern a Bangladesh consultant, i.e. tipp1239 proper, and they say only that it is tonal with low functional load and frequent glottal stops.

readall_conflicts: On stress there is no disagreement: only Chakraborty 1981 speaks of stress, and he says it is not a fixed word stress but a lexical disambiguating initial stress on particular words plus a phrase-final stress on tense/case/particle syllables; Joseph & Burling 2001 are silent on stress. On tone the two sources differ in inventory: Joseph & Burling report a two-way contrast (high vs low/falling) for Tripura Kokborok, and Matisoff's editorial footnote reports a low-functional-load 'high' tone in a Bangladesh dialect, whereas Chakraborty describes four tones (rising, falling, falling-rising, low) with no high tone and, in his introduction, even says the language is 'not tone-based'. Chakraborty's own p. 15 remark that the language is drifting from tone toward stress is consistent with Matisoff's 'low functional load'. The Veikho & Mushahary 2015 statement filed under kokb1239 ('in disyllabic words, the stress is always on the second syllable') is a fixed: final syllable claim for Indian Kokborok that would contradict Chakraborty's 'not fixed like English/Bengali' framing; it was not among this item's listed works and was not re-opened here.

sources.quote: পূর্বেই উল্লেখ করেছি যে, তিপ্রা ভাষায় ঝোঁক বর্তমান। এই ঝোঁক ইংরাজী কিংবা বাংলা ভাষার শ্বাসাঘাতের মতো নয়। [...] তিপ্রা ভাষার বাক্‌প্রবাহে শ্বাসাঘাত পড়ে দু'ভাবে। এক, শব্দবিশেষে। যেমন, 'ডিম' অর্থে |তক্তুই| বা |তাখুম্তুই| ব্যবহার না করে যদি |বুতুই| শব্দ ব্যবহার করা হয় তবে প্রায় সমোচ্চারিত 'ঝোল' বাচক |বুতুই| শব্দের সঙ্গে পৃথকীকরণের জন্য 'ডিম' বাচক |বুতুই| শব্দের আদিতে একটি ঝোঁকের ব্যবহার আবশ্যিক হয়ে পড়ে। দুই, পর্বের অন্ত্যস্বরে যদি ক্রিয়ার কাল জ্ঞাপক প্রত্যয়, কারক-বিভক্তি কিংবা অব্যয় থাকে তবে সেই অন্ত্যস্বরে একটি ঝোঁক পড়ে।
sources.locator: Ch. 1 Phonology (ধ্বনিতত্ত্ব), p. 16 (archive.org leaf 28; PDF page 28) for the stress statement; tone inventory and drift from tone to stress p. 15 (leaf 27): 'তিপ্রা ভাষায় এই স্বর এবং ঝোঁকের সন্ধান পাওয়া যায়। এবং স্বরের উপর শব্দের অর্থ-পার্থক্য কখনও কখনও নির্ভর করে।' and 'লক্ষণীয় তিপ্রা ভাষায় চারটি স্বর থাকলেও ভোট-চীনীয় ভাষার উচ্চস্বর নেই।'
sources.note: This is the same work and the same passage as the existing_statement; the quote was verified verbatim against the page scan (leaf 28, p. 16), which also corrects two scanned garbles (ঝৌক -> ঝোঁক, ম্বাসাঘাত -> শ্বাসাঘাত). The catalog record has an empty rule, so this fills it: tone language (four tones per Chakraborty) with lexical/phrase-level stress, no fixed word-stress position. Identity: the author uses 'Tipra' for the Kok-Borok dialects of the eight tribes of Tripura State (India) and did his fieldwork there (intro, pp. 3-4), so the description is of Indian Kokborok (kokb1239) rather tha…

sources.note: Sec. 4.3: generic remark that stress/accent is 'often associated with tone' in stress languages like English; Kokborok treated as tonal; no Kokborok word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Veikho, Sahiinii Lemaina & Jitamoni Mushahary. 2015. A preliminary acoustic study of vowels and tones in Kokborok. Nepalese Linguistics 30: 161-166.
sources.note: p.166 (Kokborok of Tripura, India = kokb1239): tones (high/low) assigned only to the second syllable of disyllables, first syllable default mid, 'The reason for this in Kokborok is that, in disyllabic words, the stress is always on the second syllable.' Not specific to Bangladesh Tippera.

sources.citation: Chakraborty, Santosh Kumar. 1981 [Glottolog: 1982, D.Phil. thesis Univ. of Burdwan]. A Study of Tipra Language (তিপ্রা ভাষা পরিক্রমা). Agartala: Tribal Research and Cultural Institute, Govt. of Tripura. 112 pp. In Bengali.
sources.note: pp.14-16: Tipra has both tone (স্বর; four pitch patterns claimed, meaning 'sometimes' depends on tone) and stress (ঝোঁক/শ্বাসাঘাত); stress is said to be gaining over tone. p.16: Tipra stress is NOT like English (each word its own stress) or Bengali (word-initial); in connected speech stress falls (1) on particular words, word-initially, to keep near-homophones apart (bútui 'egg' vs butui 'broth'), and (2) on the final vowel of a breath-group when that vowel belongs to a tense suffix, case ending or particle. No fixed word-stress position given; no secondary stress.
